rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage says that none of the caliphs completed the Qur’an except ʿUthmān.
rows.anchor: لم يختمه أحد من الخلفاء غير عثمان

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī swore that ʿAlī entered his grave without having memorized the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: سمعت الشعبي يحلف بالله، عز وجل، لقد دخل علي حفرته وما حفظ القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated prophetic stories let scattered tribes, each taught different sūras, hear the accounts of all the prophets and retain their warning.
rows.anchor: فلو لم تكن الأنباء والقصص مثناة ومكررة لوقعت قصة موسى إلى قوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stories differ from prescribed duties: the Prophet’s letters taught prayer, alms, fasting, and pilgrimage details that stories could not convey.
rows.anchor: وليست القصص كالفروض، لأن كتب رسول الله، صلى الله عليه وسلم كانت تنفذ إلى كل قوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This repetition served early Islam; after the religion spread, elders taught the young, and the Qur’an was collected, its rationale disappeared.
rows.anchor: فلما نشره الله عز وجل في كل قطر، وبثه في آفاق الأرض، وعلم الأكابر الأصاغر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic repeats speech for emphasis and understanding, and varies topics rather than restricting a speaker to one mode; examples include Sūrat al-Kāfirūn and al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: ومن مذاهبهم التكرار: إرادة التوكيد والإفهام، كما أن من مذاهبهم الاختصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating an oath such as ‘By God, I will not do it’ reinforces resolve; saying ‘By God, I will do it’ with an implied negation is concise.
rows.anchor: والله لا أفعله، ثم والله لا أفعله. إذا أراد التوكيد وحسم الأطماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s oath by the alphabet honors its letters as the building blocks of revealed books, divine names and attributes, and human speech and worship.
rows.anchor: وإنما أقسم الله بحروف المعجم، لشرفها وفضلها، ولأنها مباني كتبه المنزلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath by the pen magnifies what people write; the fig and olive are named for two holy-land mountains that grow them, called in Syriac Ṭūr Zaytā and Ṭūr Tīnā.
rows.anchor: وأقسم بالقلم، إعظاما لما يسطرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The detached opening letters function as oaths for the Qur’an: for example, Alif Lām Mīm means ‘By the letters, this is surely the Book’; other openings are read similarly.
rows.anchor: كأنه قال: وحروف المعجم، لهو الكتاب لا ريب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the opening letters abbreviate divine attributes, this follows Arab shorthand: words replace related words, and letters replace others with nearby articulation, as in مدهته for مدحته and جدث/جدف.
rows.anchor: وإن كان حروفا مأخوذة من صفات الله، فهذا فن من اختصار العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fragment glosses تصفر as being empty of affection.
rows.anchor: تصفر: تخلو من المحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: المكفوفة means المشرجة: folded over; Shammākh’s verse uses مشرج for what is concealed within the chest.
rows.anchor: قال الشماخ : وكادت غداة البين ينطق طرفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Prophet’s phrase about finding his Lord’s نفس from Yemen, نفس means relief, which came to him through the Anṣār.
rows.anchor: أجد نفس ربكم من قبل اليمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind’s being from the Merciful’s نفس means God relieves distress through it; the wind brought relief on the night of the Confederates.
rows.anchor: لا تسبوا الريح فإنها من نفس الرحمن

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar likewise said that the wind is from God’s روح and should not be cursed.
rows.anchor: تقول عمر رضي الله عنه: الريح من روح الله فلا تسبوها

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr’s ‘handful of God’s handfuls’ means that even if numerous, they are few before God, like what a person holds in one hand; حفنة is a handful given or taken.
rows.anchor: وقول أبي بكر رضي الله عنه: نحن حفنة من حفنات الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain ʿUmar’s proverb as ‘perhaps the little cave hides misfortunes’; it is attributed to Bihays, who killed his brothers’ murderers in a cave and was then pursued for vengeance.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضهم: هو تصغير غار. وهو مثل للعرب. ويقال: إن أول من قاله بيهس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes al-Ghuwayr to be a water source rather than a small cave.
rows.anchor: ويقال: الغوير: ماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlī’s saying that one whose father has many sons can gird himself with them means many brothers provide protection; the belt symbolizes support for the back.
rows.anchor: وقول علي كرم الله وجه: من يطل هن أبيه ينتطق به

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet illustrates the proverb with al-Ḥārith ibn Sadūs, who had twenty-one sons, as an example of strength through many brothers.
rows.anchor: قول الشاعر : فلو شاء ربي كان أير أبيكم

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar’s rule is that an emir’s pledge made without consultation establishes neither the pledger nor the pledged as ruler, since both could be killed; authority requires a public gathering’s agreement.
rows.anchor: وقول عمر رضي الله عنه: أيما رجل بايع عن غير مشاورة، فلا يؤمر واحد منهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem’s izār means the woman herself; more generally, izār is used for chastity because the chaste person is figuratively covered.
rows.anchor: وقد علقت دم القتيل إزارها أي نفسها. ويقولون للعفاف: إزار

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: ʿAdī ibn Zayd’s صلب وإزار means lineage and chastity; ṣulb refers to kin and human creation from the loins, or to a man’s family as his support.
rows.anchor: قال عدي بن زيد : أجل أن الله قد فضلكم

words: وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling night a garment means that it covers and screens the eyes; Dhu al-Rumma’s image of night dyeing the stones shows darkness as a covering.
rows.anchor: قال ذو الرمة : ودويه مثل السماء اعتسفتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Garment and clothing can metaphorically name whatever covers and protects; a poet’s ‘garment of Ibn Bayḍ’ refers either to a camel or a payment that blocked pursuers.
rows.anchor: وقد يكنون باللباس والثوب عما ستر ووقى، لأن اللباس والثوب واقيان ساتران

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī says Ibn Bayḍ slaughtered his camel on a mountain pass, blocking the route and giving rise to the saying that he blocked the road.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: (ابن بيض) رجل نحر بعيرا له على ثنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Ibn Bayḍ owed a levy, left its payment on the road to stop his pursuer, then returned and said he had blocked the road.
rows.anchor: وقال غير الأصمعي: (ابن بيض) رجل كانت عليه إتاوة فهرب بها

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some interpreters take night as stillness and spouses as stillness, supported by verses saying people rest at night and a spouse is made so one may rest with her.
rows.anchor: وكان بعض المفسرين يقول في قوله عز وجل: وهو الذي جعل لكم الليل لباسا [الفرقان: 47] أي سكنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s mercy here means Paradise, which believers enter through His mercy.
rows.anchor: يعني جنته، سماها رحمة، لأن دخولهم إياها كان برحمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سبب originally means rope, then any means of reaching a place or need; it can mean a road, a connection of kinship or affection, or a route to heaven, as in 18:85 and 40:36–37.
rows.anchor: السبب أصله: الحبل. ثم قيل لكل شيء وصلت به إلى موضع، أو حاجة تريدها: سبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s rope means His covenant or Book: hold fast to it because it connects people to God and Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال الله عز وجل: واعتصموا بحبل الله

words: إِلَّا بِحَبْلٍۢ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَحَبْلٍۢ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here a rope from God or people means safety, which gives the frightened person freedom to move wherever desired.
rows.anchor: قال الله تعالى: ضربت عليهم الذلة أين ما ثقفوا إلا بحبل من الله وحبل من الناس

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s image of one tribe’s ropes being replaced by another’s uses ropes for the bonds or guarantees that connect people and grant safety.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعشى : وإذا تجوزها حبال قبيلة

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays’s joined ropes mean joining himself to another; the image comes from tying together the ropes of two separated camels.
rows.anchor: وأما قول امرئ القيس : إني بحبلك واصل حبلي

rows.speaker: أبو زبيد
rows.claim: Abū Zubayd compares an entire night’s continuous journey to a stretched rope, explaining the expression كحبل العادية الممدود.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زبيد يذكر رجلا سرى ليلة كلها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan places the panic at resurrection: people are seized from their graves, cannot escape, and their late belief in Muḥammad or repentance cannot be accepted.
rows.anchor: كان الحسن- رضي الله عنه- يجعل الفزع يوم القيامة إذا بعثوا من القبور

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: For al-Ḥasan, the ‘distant place’ is the distance between Judgment Day and the worldly place where deeds and repentance could be accepted; their former disbelief makes faith useless.
rows.anchor: وقد كفروا به من قبل، أي بمحمد، صلى الله عليه وسلم. يقول: كيف ينفعهم الإيمان به في الآخرة

rows.speaker: غير الحسن
rows.claim: Other interpreters place the panic when God’s punishment or death arrives, citing the people who professed faith only after seeing the punishment.
rows.anchor: وكان غير الحسن يجعل الفزع عند نزول بأس الله من الموت أو غيره

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes define the extended shadow as the interval from dawn until sunrise; the unending shade of Paradise is offered as a parallel.
rows.anchor: امتداد الظل ما بين طلوع الفجر إلى طلوع الشمس. كذلك قال المفسرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God wished, He could have made the shadow permanently still like Paradise’s shade, which the sun never replaces.
rows.anchor: ولو شاء لجعله ساكنا أي: مستقرا دائما حتى يكون كظل الجنة الذي لا تنسخه الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rising sun reveals the shadow and its meaning: things are known by opposites, as with light and darkness, truth and falsehood, and paired colors and tastes; 51:49 names created pairs.
rows.anchor: وكل الأشياء تعرف بأضدادها، فلولا الشمس ما عرف الظل، ولولا النور ما عرفت الظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author’s preferred reading has God withdraw the extended shadow after sunset, gradually replacing each part with a part of night; this subtle alternation displays divine power and care for creatures and lands.
rows.anchor: وإنما يقبض الله جل وعز ذلك الظل قبضا خفيا شيئا بعد شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers يسيرا to mean subtly or gradually, since shadow and darkness do not change all at once.
rows.anchor: وقوله: قبضا يسيرا أي: خفيا، لأن الظل بعد غروب الشمس لا يذهب كله دفعة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says the sun’s superseding the shadow is its withdrawal, and يسيرا means an easy, light act for God; the author finds the first reading more comprehensive and closer to the intent.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم يجعل قبض الظل عند نسخ الشمس إياه، ويجعل قوله قبضا يسيرا أي: سهلا خفيفا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Early Muslims, scrupulous after the ban on wrongful consumption, avoided shared meals: blind people feared taking too much and others feared shorting them; the lame needed space, while illness might spoil food.
rows.anchor: فكان الأعمى لا يؤاكل الناس، لأنه لا يبصر الطعام فيخاف أن يستأثر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report through Abū Ṣāliḥ, takes the verse as removing the disabled people’s concern about eating with others.
rows.anchor: وهو معنى قول ابن عباس في رواية أبي صالح

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that campaigners gave house keys to disabled people and permitted them to eat there, but they refrained until this verse came down; al-Zuhrī and others adopt this account.
rows.anchor: وأما عائشة رضي الله عنها، فإنها قالت: كان المسلمون يوعبون مع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Your own houses’ can mean the property of one’s dependents and wives.
rows.anchor: ولا على أنفسكم أن تأكلوا من بيوتكم أراد: ولا عليكم أنفسكم أن تأكلوا من أموال عيالكم وأزواجكم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others say the phrase means children’s homes: children are their parents’ earnings and their property is like the parents’ own; the verse lists more distant kin but omits children.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أراد: أن تأكلوا من بيوت أولادكم، فنسب بيوت الأولاد إلى الآباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s statement about the star is a staged argument: he feigns the community’s reverence to gain their trust, then shows that a setting star cannot be God and applies the lesson to moon and sun without provocation.
rows.anchor: يريد: أن يستدرجهم بهذا القول، ويعرفهم خطأهم، وجهلهم في تعظيمهم شأن النجوم

words: إِنِّى وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِىَ لِلَّذِى فَطَرَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham directs himself to the Creator of the heavens and earth and everything within them, declaring his separation from the people’s associations.
rows.anchor: إني وجهت وجهي للذي فطر السماوات وما فيها من نجم وقمر وشمس والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares Abraham’s strategy to a ḥawārī who feigned devotion to an idol, exposed its inability to help against an enemy, and then led its worshippers to pray to God, who delivered them.
rows.anchor: ومثل هذا: الحواري حين ورد على قوم يعبدون (بدا) لهم فأظهر تعظيمه

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: Some claim Abraham was then in error and confusion; Ibn Qutayba rejects this because God protected and purified him, citing his sound heart and exegetes who say he never associated anything with God.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من يذهب إلى أن إبراهيم صلى الله عليه وسلم، كان في تلك الحال على ضلال وحيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s command to the mountains and birds to awbī with David means to praise with him, in keeping with the statement that all things glorify God though people do not understand their praise.
rows.anchor: يا جبال أوبي معه والطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell nearly bursting from rage is an idiom for almost splitting with anger; the cited report says it cries قط قط, meaning ‘enough’.
rows.anchor: وقال في جهنم: تكاد تميز من الغيظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ants are among the الحكل, creatures without audible voices; Ruʾba’s verse uses الحكل to name the kind of speech Solomon understood.
rows.anchor: قال رؤية : لو كنت قد أوتيت علم الحكل

rows.speaker: العماني
rows.claim: Al-ʿUmānī says the discerning man understands even a particle’s secret exchange; السواد means whispered speech because these creatures do not make a sound.
rows.anchor: وقال العماني يمدح رجلا :

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was told by the poisoned arm and by a camel that its owners starved and overworked it, among other examples of animals communicating.
rows.anchor: وهذا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، تخبره الذراع المسمومة ويخبره البعير أن أهله يجيعونه ويدئبونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who dismissed magic except as trickery nevertheless described spells that separate spouses, lies that change affection, and poisons affecting sexual ability or appearance; the Qur’an confirms blowing into knots, like light spitting.
rows.anchor: والله تعالى يقول: ومن شر النفاثات في العقد

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poet’s ‘her glance ties Babylonian magic’ means her eyes captivate the mind as magic or wine does.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : يعقد سحر البابليين طرفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was bewitched and the spell placed in the well of Dhū Arwān; ʿAlī extracted it and untied its knots one by one, each bringing relief until the Prophet recovered.
rows.anchor: وقد سحر رسول الله، صلى الله عليه وسلم، وجعل سحره في بئر ذي أروان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajm originally means throwing; the stars are called missiles against devils.
rows.anchor: أصله الرمي، كقوله تعالى: وجعلناها رجوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajm figuratively means killing because people were killed by stoning; the first murder was reportedly by stones, so the term later applied even without stones.
rows.anchor: ثم يستعار فيوضع موضع القتل، لأنهم كانوا يقتلون بالرجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajm can mean insult: abuse is verbal throwing, as is also reflected in the root meaning of qadhf.
rows.anchor: وأصل القذف: الرمي، ومنه قول أبي إبراهيم له: لأرجمنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajm also means conjecture, as in rajman bi al-ghayb: one figuratively throws a guess.
rows.anchor: ويوضع موضع الظن، ومنه قوله: رجما بالغيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajm can mean cursing or expelling; rajīm describes Satan as banished, since meteors drive him away.
rows.anchor: والرجم: اللعن. والطرد: لعن، ومنه قيل: ذئب لعين: أي طريد

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar did not know Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt’s verse likening earth to a female for rain; later interpreters explain rain makes the earth bear vegetation.
rows.anchor: وحدثني أبو حاتم ، عن الأصمعي أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s imagery treats earth as female and rain as male, which fertilizes it; the same pairing is applied to firesticks, whose spark is their offspring.
rows.anchor: معناه: أن الله جعل الأرض كالأنثى للماء، وجل الماء كالذكر للأرض، فإذا مطرت أنبتت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مسفد means mated: the male si fada the female, and God caused him to mate, parallel to nakaha/ankahahu.
rows.anchor: و (مسفد) بمعنى: منكح. تقول: سفد الذكر الأنثى، والله أسفده

rows.speaker: ذو الرمة
rows.claim: In Dhu al-Rumma’s parallel verse, السقط means fire, the father is the upper firestick, and the mother is the lower firestick.
rows.anchor: وسقط كعين الديك عاورت صحبتي

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: A second Umayya poem was transmitted as عسل ما, but the author says it should read سلع ما; al-Salʿ and al-ʿUshr are trees used in rain-making rites by tying and burning them on cows’ tails.
rows.anchor: هكذا رواه عسل ما وإنما هو: سلع ما. ومعنى البيت: أنهم كانوا يستمطرون بالسلع والعشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وعالت البيقورا means a drought year burdened the cows with the ritual branches and fire; al-ʿāʾil means poor, and a second poet’s verse supports the corrected reading سلع.
rows.anchor: وقوله: (وعالت البيقورا) يعني: سنة الجدب

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī said the learned had disappeared who could explain Imruʾ al-Qays’s verse about سلكى and مخلوجة.
rows.anchor: وحدثني أيضا أبو حاتم، عن الأصمعي، أنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source continues al-Aṣmaʿī’s report, saying likewise that no one remained who understood al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza’s verse about those who struck the ʿayr.
rows.anchor: وقال مثل ذلك في بيت الحارث بن حلزة
